# Atomic

Values that threads share without a lock: atomic integers, flags and pointers.

## Installation

Add `Atomic` to the `[Dependencies]` table of your package's `Rux.toml`:

```toml
[Dependencies]
Atomic = { Namespace = "Rux", Version = "0.1.0" }
```

Standard packages are declared by hand: the registry does not serve them, so `rux add Rux/Atomic` cannot add them.

## Dependencies

- [`Core`](/docs/api/core) 0.1.0

## Guide

### What it provides

| Module                              | Covers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [`Atomic`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic) | [`Atomic<T>`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic) with [`Load`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic#load), [`Store`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic#store), [`Exchange`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic#exchange), [`CompareExchange`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic#compare-exchange) and [`FetchAdd`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic#fetch-add)/`Sub`/`And`/`Or`/`Xor`, and `With` forms that take a `MemoryOrder` |

The module names describe where each declaration comes from; they are not part of an import path.

### Example

```rux
import Atomic::Atomic;
import Core::MemoryOrder;

func Count(hits: &Atomic<uint64>) -> uint64 {
    hits.FetchAddWith(1, MemoryOrder::Relaxed);
    return hits.Load();
}
```

### Design

[`Atomic<T>`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic) holds one integer of 8 to 64 bits, `bool` or pointer and touches it only through `Core`'s atomic intrinsics, so no thread ever sees a value half written and each change is one indivisible step. Its methods take the value by shared reference, because several threads reaching it at once is the point; the hardware keeps their accesses apart. Any other `T` is refused where the methods are used.

The plain methods are sequentially consistent: every thread agrees on one order of all of them, which is never wrong. The `With` forms take a weaker `MemoryOrder` for code that has worked out it is enough, such as a relaxed counter or a release decrement of a reference count. An order an operation cannot have is strengthened to the nearest one it can, so `LoadWith(MemoryOrder::Release)` loads with `Acquire`. Because the intrinsics need their order written as a case, a `With` method selects among them; the plain methods involve no such choice.

[`CompareExchange`](/docs/api/atomic/atomic#compare-exchange) succeeds with the value it replaced and fails with the value it found, so a retry loop starts again from what is really there. It never fails spuriously.
